newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: PRESS DIGEST - CENTRAL AND EAST EUROPE - MAY 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - CENTRAL AND EAST EUROPE - MAY 21.

text.p: SLOVENIA
DELO

- Prime ministers of Hungary, Italy and Slovenia on signed an agreement on mutual cooperation in Budapest on Tuesday. The agreement expressed expectations of Slovenia and Hungary to join NATO in the first round of its expansion.
- On Thursday Slovenia's Constitutional Court is expected to say whether ratification of the EU association agreement, which was signed in June last year, was in line with the country's constitution.
- Slovenian Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler on Tuesday finnished his visit to Poland by visiting Polish Defence Minister Stanislaw Dobrzanski.

- Passenger traffic on Slovenian railways was unaffected after the first day of a 10-day strike started by railway workers, demanding increase in salaries and holiday pay. Cargo traffic will be stopped again on Wednesday.
- Slovenia's largest petrol trading company Petrol on Tuesday demanded increase in prices of different petroleum derivates between two and six percent.
- Union, one of Slovenia's two largest breweries starts its biggest investment so far. Construction of the new warehouse, which starts on Wednesday is expected to cost 55 million marks.
DNEVNIK
- Prices of new cars in Slovenia will be up to 16 percent higher from the start of July. when the new taxation law comes into effect.
VECER
- Slovenia's sales in tourism in the first three months rose by two percent to $252,466 million compared to the same period of 1996, the Bank of Slovenia said on Tuesday.
- Some 65 domestic and foreign companies participate in the sixth Security fair, which opened in Ljubljana on Tuesday.
AUSTRIA
DER STANDARD

- Conservative chief whip Andreas Khol says the senior coalition partner the Social Democrats should not move alone in a bid to improve women's rights. About 800,000 Austrians signed a petition on more women's rights earlier this year.
- Austria will not be able to reduce the greenhouse effect in the extent it had agreed to at the Toronto climate summit, as the states and the federal government cannot agree on joint measures.
- Do-It-Yourself chain bauMax plans to raise its turnover to 7.8 billion schillings this year. Bonus shares will be paid out additionally to the dividend.

- The World Economic Forum ranks Austria only as 27th concerning its competitiveness among the 53 largest industrial nations in 1997. Austria has fallen eight places since the last year. The country's market growth is only ranked 34th.
- Oil and chemicals group OMV's Hungarian unit OMV Hungaria reported losses of 35 million schillings even though turnover jumped 30 percent.
- Raiffeisen Zentralbank's operating profits jumped 22.3 percent to 2.6 billion schillings. The bank's eastern European subsidiaries accounted for over 50 percent of the profits.
DIE PRESSE
- Conservative state leaders are against the federal party's plans to join Nato as quick as possible as well as the new law restricting the politivian's renumeration.
- Both the current Interior Minister Karl Schloegl as well as his pre-decessor Caspar Einem did not know about the police finding numerous arms depots of the Soviet secret service KGB.
- Chancellor Viktor Klima and Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger say the government plans to raise public pensions in 1998 by 1.5 percent at the most.
- Former Justice Minister Egmont Foregger says the escape of the alleged Iranian murderers of three Kurdish leaders in 1989 happened due to unfortunate circumstances.
- The concept of the government's new exporting offensive is ready and will be discussed at the government's convention at the beginning of June.
- The number of new car registrations also went back in April.
KURIER
- Austria is on the search for alleged investments of former Zairian dictator Mobutu in Austria.
- Conservatives plan to discuss the abolition of the country's conscription should Austria join NATO.

- Raiffeisen Zentralbank wants to take over all the available shares of Bank Austria in Investkredit and Kontrollbank. The bank favours insurance holding BARC to buy the government's stake in postal savings bank PSK. However, it says it would also participate itself should this not be possible.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- The Conservatives say the Social Democrats plan to include all workers in the social security system would cost job. About 165,000 Austrians would have to start paying social security fees.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- The government has not started paying out the money it plans to subsise technological research with as the laws have not been made for it yet.
SLOVAKIA
NARODNA OBRODA - The National Bank of Slovakia on Tuesday fixed the crown stronger against the market showing its commitment to support the currency if neccessary, dealers said.

- Interior Minister Gustav Krajci has asked President Michal Kovac to postpone referendum on direct presidential elections until the Constitutional Court rules on the request by deputies of ruling whether the constitution can be changed by a referendum.
- President Kovac rejected Krajci's request saying the referendum must be carried out regardless of what will be the Constitutional Court ruling.

- Rudolf Schuster, a Mayor of the second largest Slovak city of Kosice, eastern Slovakia, said he would submit his candidacy in next year's presidential elections if the planned referendum instals a direct citizens vote of the president.
- The Czech engineering company CKD Praha said it would present its project for building an undergroung transport system in the Slovak capital Bratislava.
- The Slovak governemnt on Tuesday approved a draft law which should enable the state to impose unspecified measures to limit imports of goods that are also produced in Slovakia.

PRAVDA - The paper quotes ruling coalition sources as saying some deputies of two minor coalition parties, the ultra-left Workers Party (ZRS) and the extreme-right Slovak National party (SNS), wanted a dismissal of the National Property Fund President Stefan Gavornik and the Minister of Justice Jozef Liscak.

- Parliamentary Chairman Ivan Gasparovic said the ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) wanted citizens to vote in favour of NATO membership in a referendum on the question scheduled for next weekend.

- The Constitutional Court is expected to rule on Wednesday on the request by deputies of ruling coalition whether the consitution can be changed by a referendum. Deputies submitted the request in an atempt to cancel the referendum on direct presidential elections.

- President Michal Kovac said a negative answer in a referendum on NATO membership would be a "catastrophe" for Slovakia, since the result of the plebiscite would be valid for the next three years without any chance for the government or the parliament to change it.
SME - Major Slovak opposition parties have repeatedly called for citizens to vote "yes" both for integration in NATO and direct presidential elections.
HOSPODARSKE NOVINY - Production of the Slovak engineering sector should total some 99 billion crowns a year in 2000 rising further to 161.6 billion crowns in the year 2005.
BOSNIA
DNEVNI AVAZ

- The High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, plans to request that the international commununity refuse to recognise any Bosnian ambassador who is not appointed by the collective presidency by July 1, diplomatic sources say.
OSLOBODJENJE
- Dividing the assets of former Yugoslavia is a complex issue, but it should be resolved soon, says Sir Arthur Watts, special negotiator for succession.

- The ombudsmen for the Moslem-Croat federation publish report on human rights violations which says the majority of abuses were committed by government authorities over tenancy rights to state-owned property.
- The crime rate in the Moslem-Croat federation decreased in April while suicides and car accidents increased, federation interior ministry says.
- A mass grave containing the bodies of 171 Moslem and Croats killed in 1992 has been discovered in the village of Hrgar in the Bihac region, interior ministry says.
- The Nato-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) was ready to arrest indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic last week but he did not dare leave his home, anonymous sources tell newspaper.

- The U.S. Agency for International Development has been granted 200 million dollars to assist Bosnian companies which will be dispersed after Washington reviews how Bosnian factions are complying with the Dayton peace treaty, says U.S. official.
